cards.title: Write a five-part business plan for a store launch or reposition
cards.summary: Replace the boilerplate business plan with five sections—Truth, Assertions, Alternatives, People, Money—so a store's direction and assumptions are testable before you spend on inventory and ads.
cards.use_when: Planning a new product line, store launch, brand repositioning or annual plan and you need an honest internal document rather than an investor compliance exercise.
steps: Write the Truth section first: the market you're entering, the needs that exist, competitors in your space, technology standards, and how others have succeeded and failed. Footnote if useful, but keep it non-partisan—no positions, just how things are. Include market share analysis, spreadsheets and visceral customer stories. The goal is that you and your team agree on the assumptions.

Write Assertions: 'We will do X, and then Y will happen.' Name the specific market you serve and the change you expect on arrival. This is the heart of the plan and it will be partly wrong—budgets, deadlines and sales will miss.

Write Alternatives so a missed assertion isn't fatal: how much flexibility does your product, supply chain or team have? If the assertion doesn't pan out, what's next? This is what lets you test rather than bet the store.
Write People: not resumes but attitudes, abilities and track record in shipping. Include who you serve, who your champions are, what they believe about status, and what worldview they hold.
Write Money last: capital needed, how you'll spend it, cash flow, P&L, balance sheet, margins, exit.

Treat your 'why' or mission statement as not the deliverable. The source argues most purposes reduce to 'sell more of what I already decided to sell.' The plan's job is to make the universal need specific: who it's for, what tension you create, what status roles you engage, and the story that makes change happen.
caveats: The source concedes this format may not satisfy a local VC; it's framed as a thinking tool for your team, not an investor deck.
A failed assertion doesn't mean the business lacks purpose—it rules out one route and frees you to find another.

cards.title: Choose dominion or affiliation status signals for your customers
cards.summary: Customers read your store through either a vertical dominance lens (winners/losers) or a horizontal affiliation lens (insiders/outsiders), and the customer's worldview, not yours, determines which works.
cards.use_when: Deciding brand voice, creative direction and community mechanics for a store—especially when you must pick between aggressive competitive positioning and belonging-based positioning.
steps: Determine which status worldview your customers already hold. Dominion is vertical—above or below, winning and losing, 'who eats first.' Affiliation is horizontal—'who's standing next to me,' insiders and outsiders, being in sync with the group.

If you market to dominion: accept that some customers, partners and employees respond to a narrative of winning and losing. The source points to Uber's early years—contentious relationships with governments, competitors and drivers—as dominance signaling that let aligned investors, employees and users double down on the story.

If you market to affiliation: send signals of who else is here. Trade-show booth traffic, who attends the launch, who blurbed the book—all shorthand for 'are people like us doing something like this?' Prime the pump with the right signals to the right people to start a cascade.

Adapt affiliation tactics by business type as the source suggests: B2B sellers build referrals; a local craftsperson hunkers down in a single neighborhood until reputation is assured; investment banks run tombstone ads listing the 'right' firms.

Note that affiliation tolerates abundance (more affiliation helps everyone) while dominion leans on scarcity. Fashion, per the source, is usually affiliation: the leader's role is providing a signal that everyone else will be in sync—the goal isn't winning, it's being part of the group.

Test which frame your audience actually uses before committing spend; the source warns that people aligned with one worldview often can't imagine choosing the other, so internal consensus is not evidence.
caveats: The source states the customer's worldview is always stronger than the story you choose to tell—this is positioning guidance, not a claim that dominance messaging fails.
Uber is given as an example of aligned signaling, not a validated long-term brand outcome.

cards.title: Use semiotics so your store reminds buyers of the right thing
cards.summary: Shoppers scan rather than study, asking 'what does this remind me of?', so logos, page styling, photography and packaging should be engineered to trigger the associations you want before anyone reads your copy.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing a storefront, PDP photography, packaging, email design or ad creative where first-impression trust is at stake.
steps: Accept the scanning reality: with too many choices and everything 'good enough,' busy people don't study your work, don't know your competitive drama, and don't care how hard you worked. They ask what it reminds them of.

Audit your signals for unwanted associations. The source's examples: a site that feels like GeoCities with flashing GIFs, or a call with telltale clicks and pauses that reads as robocall and gets hung up before a word is spoken. If you remind someone of a scam, undoing that first impression takes a long time.

Choose signals that fit your category's trust code. Big companies' logos often look alike not from laziness but because designers are trying to remind you of a solid company. A summer blockbuster gives itself away in four frames—it's clearly not a teen makeup guru's YouTube video.

Hire a professional when the stakes justify it, because the professional designs what other people will like, not what you like. The source allows that an amateur occasionally stumbles onto the right vernacular, but says the rest of the time it's best done with intent.

Remember the symbol lives in the viewer's mind, not yours: a hoodie signals status in Silicon Valley ('too busy to shop') but may put someone in East London on alert. There is no single right answer—the symbol that works for one group won't for another.
Be aware that flags and flares get copied until they stop being scarce and become mere signals of changing taste, so what reads as premium today can drift.
caveats: Semiotic readings can encode bias—the Witchsy.com case is cited, where a fictitious male partner 'Keith' got faster, more helpful vendor and developer replies than the real female founders. The source says marketers should acknowledge the culture they seek to change rather than deny it.
Semiotics is a design and trust heuristic; the source offers no measurement method.

cards.title: Fly a specific flag instead of claiming no brand identity
cards.summary: A brand is the customer's shorthand for what you promise, and the smallest viable market means the right flag is a narrow, deliberate choice—not a message broad enough for everyone.
cards.use_when: Running brand positioning work, naming a store, writing taglines or choosing the aesthetic that determines who self-selects into your customer base.
steps: Define a brand as the customer's expectation: what promise do they think you're making when they buy, meet you or hire you? That promise—not your logo—is the brand. The source contrasts a true brand with a commodity (wheat by the ton, coffee by the pound, bandwidth by the GB), where no expectation exists beyond spec: same as yesterday, faster and cheaper.

Accept that you cannot build a brand for everyone. Be specific, be very specific, then overdo your brand marketing on that narrow target. Every slice of every interaction should reflect the whole: from any one touchpoint, a customer should be able to make a smart guess about all of you.

Choose a flag with intent, because not flying one is as intentional as flying one. Customers are trying to figure out who you are; make it easy for them to know who you are and where you stand. The source calls the lazy move insisting you don't need a flag and the foolish move pretending your features are so good nothing else matters.

Send a signal that feels like a sign customers already trust, then change it enough to show it's new and yours—this is the same-and-different principle. Apple's 1984 ad only needed a million people to care, targeting the media-savvy and the nerds first, ignoring everyone else; the source notes the idea took about thirty years to spread outward.

Don't overinvest in the logo itself: logos matter less than designers want but more than committees realize. Make it work at different sizes in different media, avoid offending or distracting people, then pick one, don't spend a lot of money or hold many meetings about it, and keep it as long as your first name.

Expect tension between going first (innovation reminds some people of a past failure) and reaching the market that will actually give a new thing a chance—start with the audience that tolerates that association.
caveats: The Apple 1984 example is presented as a semiotic case, not a replicable playbook, and its results are described as a 30-year compounding outcome.
The source asserts logos of mediocre brands can still work and great brands can lack memorable logos, so logo spend is often overrated.

cards.title: Aim new products at neophiliacs first, not the whole market
cards.summary: Roughly the left tail of the distribution actively seeks novelty, and the source argues that spending time or money trying to convert satisfied customers is wasted until the idea reaches them peer-to-peer.
cards.use_when: Deciding who to seed a new product, launch, bundle or category with first, and how to allocate launch marketing budget.
steps: Use the distribution as a rough mental model for any group: about 68% cluster near the average, 27% sit significantly further out, and a few are extreme outliers. For style, technology and innovations, most people like what they have and want to do what others are doing.

Identify the early adopters—those who will queue for opening night, upgrade their operating system immediately, and read Vogue for the ads. The source frames this as the left side of the curve and says not to waste a minute of your time or theirs on anyone who isn't there.

Skip the direct-conversion attempt on satisfied customers. The source's reasoning is arithmetic, not moral: if someone is content, you likely don't have the time or money to make them dissatisfied enough, interested enough and open enough to switch—not right now.
Reach the holdouts horizontally, person-to-person through earned media, with persistence and smarts. That's an eventual path, not a launch tactic.

Design the offer for what neophiliacs actually want: to go first, hope and possibility and magic, the thrill of it working and the risk it might not, the pleasure of showing innovation to the crew, and the satisfaction of doing better work faster.

Segment by desire rather than demographics. The source lists different wants among the same market: the corporate buyer wants to avoid trouble and have an alibi; the social crusader wants a glimmer of hope and a chance to make things right; the dominance-seeker wants to win; the affiliation-seeker wants to fit in without the risk of being picked to lead; some want a bargain and a few eagerly overpay to prove they can; almost no one wants to feel stupid.
caveats: The 68/27/4 percentages describe standard deviation in a measured population; the source uses them as a behavioral heuristic, not a store-specific conversion model.
The instruction not to market to the middle is a marketing-resource argument, not a claim that satisfied customers never buy.

cards.title: Earn enrollment instead of buying attention
cards.summary: Enrollment is voluntary education—customers eagerly lending attention because they expect insight or forward motion—and the source frames it as the consensual first step of a mutual journey.
cards.use_when: Designing launch content, email opt-ins, community or loyalty programs, and deciding what you offer in exchange for a shopper's attention.
steps: Treat mandatory education as impossible; there's no teaching people against their will. Aim instead for enrollment: hands raised, eyes on the board, notes being taken.
Make the exchange explicit: they lend attention because they'll get the insight or forward motion they want. Enrollment leads to change and to permission to keep engaging.

Avoid buying enrollment with flashy ads; the source calls that the lazy route. The best marketers earn it by seeking people who want the change on offer, and by connecting those people to others who want the change as well.
Use enrollment as the first step in a two-way journey: you learn from the customer and she learns from you. This distinguishes it from a one-shot acquisition push.

Sequence it in the marketing chain the source describes: an ad exists to get a click; the click exists to make a sale or earn permission; the sale exists to lead to another sale or word of mouth; permission exists to lead to education and then a sale. If you offer education content instead of a hard sell, know which rung of that chain it sits on.

Target people who want what the education delivers—not everyone wants responsibility, some want recognition, and many want convenience so they don't have to pay attention or exercise judgment. The source's instruction is to always be wondering, testing and willing to treat different people differently, because if you don't, they'll find someone who will.
caveats: The source gives no conversion benchmarks for enrollment, so treat the mutual-journey claim as a framing principle rather than a measured funnel.
It warns against bribing attention with flashy ads, which is a resource-allocation opinion, not proof that paid acquisition fails.

cards.title: Identify and multiply overinvest in your superusers
cards.summary: Everyone has a publishing platform now, but not everyone uses it, so the profitable move is to watch who actually advocates for you and give those people something worth talking about.
cards.use_when: Designing reviewer, UGC, refer-a-friend, ambassador or loyalty programs and deciding where to concentrate service and perks.
steps: Reject the flat 'everyone is a critic now, so treat everyone better' logic. The source argues the math doesn't hold: treating everyone better with fixed resources is a bit like treating everyone worse—you can't treat everyone better than you already are.

Watch behavior instead of stated intent. Everyone could be a neophiliac, a sneezer or a power user; only some take the opportunity. Look at who is actually adopting your cause, talking about you, or trying to lead.

Adopt them back. When someone is eager to talk about what you do, give them something to talk about. When someone itches to be a generous leader, give her the resources to lead. The source notes the technical levers exist to treat different people differently if you choose.

Ground the prioritization in contribution economics: your fixed costs—suits, storefront, software, inventory, ads, publicity and a hundred other things—spread across the whole customer base. The source's graph shows gross margin earned per customer against the per-person marketing spend line, with only eight customers on the graph actually contributing profit.

Extend that to service. A valuable customer in a support queue may be identifiable in the record: years of tenure, deposits, tweeting about you, no returns, on-time payment, high-margin purchases, producing far more revenue than the average. For that customer, the source endorses extraordinary acts—drive across town, get the shipment into the last FedEx pickup, have the CEO call the person you triple-charged—because the cost of being human is covered by the upside of delighting an extraordinary customer.
Ask what the interaction is for before defaulting to scripts. If the goal is to get it over with, deny responsibility and cite policy, the source says keep doing that and watch it all fall apart.
Accept that you can't do this for every customer, but you can learn to see and act accordingly. Serve many; profit from a few—the whales pay for the minnows.
caveats: The 'eight of the customers on this graph' figure is a hypothetical illustration of the fixed-cost math, not a benchmark for any store.
The source explicitly permits treating different customers differently rather than trying to treat everyone equally well; that conflicts with absolute service-equality policies some operators hold.

cards.title: Separate goal, strategy and tactics before running campaigns
cards.summary: A goal is the change you seek, strategy is the durable way you invest toward it, and tactics are the hundreds of replaceable steps—confusing the three makes stores abandon working strategies when a tactic underperforms.
cards.use_when: Setting annual marketing direction, deciding whether to drop a channel, or aligning a team on what counts as failure.
steps: Write the goal as the change in the world or in those you serve, not the self-focused goal of earning money. It's the shining light and unwavering destination.

Write strategy as the long-lasting way you invest toward that goal. The source offers examples: earn trust and attention; be seen as the best and maybe only alternative; build alliances and partnerships that reach exactly the right people. Using stories, status and connection to create tension and forward motion is itself a strategy.
List tactics as the dozens or hundreds of steps supporting the strategy. If a tactic fails, another can take its place—tactics can be changed the moment they stop helping.
Test strategy changes rarely, not reactively. If a strategy fails you may need to change it, but you don't want to do so often.

Learn from the contrast: Coca-Cola's goal was more people drinking more Coke, its strategy an enormous volume of mass-market ads tying Coke to happiness and everyone else drinking it, while each individual ad's content was a replaceable tactic. Patagonia's goal keeps a small group of outdoor enthusiasts caring for the environment and expressing it through apparel; the strategy has been stable for more than thirty years—redefining how some people think about environmental impact and clothing quality, giving a small group a label and a tool to evangelize, creating insiders and outsiders—while tactics range from clothes recycling to brick buildings to material, selection and price choices.

Use the test of disclosure: if you tell a competitor your tactics, they'll steal them and it costs you; telling them your strategy doesn't matter, because they lack the guts or persistence to convert it into their own.
caveats: The source is explicit that strategy talk is a guardrail against tactic churn; it does not supply metrics for when a strategy should be retired.
Coca-Cola and Patagonia are illustrative cases, not templates to copy.

cards.title: Decide whether to buy ads at all—and which kind
cards.summary: Online advertising is simultaneously the most precise, instant and measurable channel ever and the most ignored, so the source says buy direct only when you can measure every step, and buy brand only if you can be patient and consistent.
cards.use_when: Allocating budget between paid acquisition and brand-building, or judging whether a paid channel should be scaled or killed.
steps: Use the three genuine advantages of online ads: precision (psychographics—what people believe and want—not just demographics), instantaneity (decide at 10 a.m., reach people at 10:01 a.m.), and measurement.

Weigh the cost side the source stresses: it is not unusual to run an ad in front of a hundred thousand people and get not a single click, or to start, run and finish an entire campaign without moving the culture. Advertising is unearned media and recipients know it—they're suspicious, inundated and exhausted, so you're ignored.

Understand the price-attention equation before buying. The source contrasts a fancy magazine at about $80 CPM (roughly a dime per reader) with an $80 placement in front of a million people on a second-rate site where readers are scanning and clicking past—those people won't remember the ad or act.

If buying direct, measure everything: compute the cost to earn attention, the cost per click, and the cost to turn that attention into an order. The chain is: ad exists to get a click; click exists to make a sale or earn permission; sale exists to lead to another sale or word of mouth; permission exists to lead to education and to a sale. Assign values to each step, and if you can't, the source says don't run any direct-response ads until you can.

If buying brand, be patient and refuse to measure, engaging with the culture instead. Brand marketing is culturally oriented and can't be measured; direct is action-oriented and measured. The source warns the danger is confusing the two.

Fund brand work only from what you can sustain: you're already spending on brand marketing through phone manner, packaging, location, hold music, executive behavior and packing peanuts. Be consistent and patient, and if you can't afford to be consistent and patient, don't pay for brand marketing ads.

Note how the economics differ by size: Google's and Facebook's revenue growth comes from ads that pay for themselves—$100 of online advertising generating $125 in profit means buying more until ads stop paying—while many large brand advertisers (Ford, Absolut, Palmolive; P&G's Tide and Crest on TV) can't construct direct campaigns that work, and local businesses hooked on Yellow Pages struggle to move to review platforms that feel uncontrolled and unproven.
caveats: The $80 CPM and $100-to-$125 examples are illustrations of the math, not benchmarks for any product category.
Google, Facebook and Meta ad interfaces and measurement options change frequently; verify current capabilities and attribution in the ad platform before relying on any specific setup.
The instruction to 'refuse to measure' brand marketing is the source's opinion and conflicts with common practice—hold brand and direct to different standards rather than applying the same scorecard.

cards.title: Build frequency before judging a message dead
cards.summary: People trust what they rehearse, so campaigns that seem stale to you may only just be landing with your market—quitting during the dip forfeits the trust the repetition was building.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to refresh ad creative, retire a tagline, change a packaging story or abandon a channel that hasn't produced results yet.
steps: Accept the memory reality: people don't remember what they read, hear or even see, and aren't good at remembering what they do. We remember what we rehearse—what we see again and again. The familiar is normal and the normal is trusted.

Expect the dip: there's a very real gap between when the marketer gets bored and when the audience gets the message. The source's pattern is people giving a talk a few times and moving on, launching a freelance practice and quitting when it sputters, or raising money and spending fast, hitting the wall just before the good stuff happens.

Apply the Jay Levinson standard the source quotes: don't change your ads when you're tired of them, not when your employees are tired of them, not even when your friends are tired of them—change them when your accountant is tired of them.

Extend frequency beyond ads. All storytelling requires it: a new statement, a new market exploration—when it doesn't work right away the instinct is to walk away, but frequency is what earns the chance.

Differentiate deliberate consistency from blind stubbornness by using the goal/strategy/tactics split: frequency applies to the strategy and story, while individual tactics can be swapped the moment they stop supporting it.
Budget the repetition honestly before you launch, since frequency means paying for the same message multiple times rather than producing one round of creative.
caveats: The source gives no frequency threshold (such as a number of impressions or weeks) and no measurement guidance; treat frequency as a persistence principle, not a calculable target.
The Levinson line is quoted as an opinion about creative refresh timing, not a data-backed rule.

cards.title: Make your store the thing people search for by name
cards.summary: Generic search rankings can't support every business, so the durable path is building a product or service people care enough to look up specifically—then being what they find when they type your name.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in generic-term SEO, brand-name search, or marketplace and paid placement for a store with limited budget.
steps: Reject the myth that grooming your site for generic terms means searchers will find you. There are a thousand pages of results for 'tire store,' 'restaurant' or 'freelance copy editor,' and the source argues the math can't support every business imagining it will be the first match.

Recognize the unequal outcome: the locksmith, hotel or doctor who wins a generic search earns a huge profit, while everyone else spends on consultants and trickery to rank higher—a pyramid the source says the math can't support.
Reframe the objective: the path is to have someone care enough about you and what you create that they type your name, looking for you rather than a generic alternative.

Do step one—build a product or service worth searching for specifically, not for the generic term. Once that exists, Google is on your side: platforms want you to be found when someone searches for you.
Do step two—be the one they want to find when they go looking. That means owning the branded result for your name and product names, not just the category term.
Translate this into store decisions: distinctive products, ownable product names and a brand people remember are the SEO assets; generic category keywords are a bidding war, not a moat.
caveats: This is the source's argument, framed as a mathematical objection to generic SEO; it does not deny that category search can drive sales for some businesses—the source acknowledges the locksmith, hotel or doctor gains a huge profit from a generic win.
No keyword volumes, ranking factors or measurement methods are given.

cards.title: Price as positioning signal, not just revenue math
cards.summary: Price tells a story about who you are for, and the margin it creates funds the outbound marketing that gets you noticed—so the number is a positioning decision before it's a spreadsheet cell.
cards.use_when: Setting price points, launching a premium or value line, or deciding whether to compete on cheapest price.
steps: Start from the two-way rule: marketing changes your pricing, and pricing changes your marketing. People form assumptions and associations from the price, and the price shapes what they believe about the service.

Check alignment: your price should match the extremes you claimed in positioning. Note that asking who buys the cheapest or the most expensive wine says nothing about taste or value—only price, which is itself the signal. A Porsche Cayenne has no utility proportionate to its expense; it's a flag flown in the driveway and in self-esteem.

Run the margin arithmetic before choosing the position. The source's baker: costs of $1.95 per loaf at reasonable quantity yield a nickel profit at $2.00, fifty-five cents at $2.50 (an eleven-fold increase, over 1,000% more profit per loaf), and over a dollar at $3.00—more than twenty times the first example. The $2.00 baker must sell twenty-one loaves for every loaf the luxury baker sells.

Decide what the higher price is actually buying the customer, using concrete trade-offs: a sparkling clean shop, well-paid and helpful staff, a new window sign, a local baseball team in jerseys with your logo, a handsome shopping bag with every loaf, free butter-cookie samples, and the social pleasure of telling friends they're eating the same bread as the fancy restaurant down the street. The source's framing: better to apologize for the price once than to excuse a hundred small slights again and again.

Recognize that racing to be cheapest means you're not investing sufficiently in change—you're promising the same, but cheaper. The source notes the race to the bottom is tempting because nothing is easier to sell than cheaper, but that ease is the trap. (This is the source's opinion, offered with the caveat 'unless you've found an extraordinary new way to deliver your product or service.')
Remember that margin is the money available for outbound marketing—the price position and the marketing budget are one decision, not two.
caveats: The baker's cost and profit figures are an illustrative example, not a benchmark for any category.
The claim that low price signals insufficient investment in change is the source's opinion with a stated exception for genuinely novel delivery; it is not proof that low-price strategies fail.

cards.title: Handle price discrimination with story, not mechanics
cards.summary: The price tag itself was an innovation built on treating buyers equally, and the source says the hard part of variable or dynamic pricing today is the storytelling, not the implementation.
cards.use_when: Planning discounts, member pricing, dynamic pricing, flash sales, Kickstarter-style tiers or loyalty pricing—and anticipating customer reaction.
steps: Take the historical frame: Quakers originated the fixed price tag because charging different people different prices felt immoral; Macy's and Wanamaker's scaled it because they needed huge stores with low-paid staff and couldn't train or trust that many people to haggle. Industrialists liked the efficiency.

Recognize what the internet changed: on one hand, a store can tell the story that the price is the price—the source cites Tesla, whose fixed pricing luxury buyers reportedly greeted with relief. On the other, matching price to demand cost Uber billions in brand trust, per the source.
For most organizations, especially small ones, the difficulty isn't the mechanics of charging different amounts—it's the storytelling.

Anticipate the emotional questions customers ask: how do you feel when you discover you got a discount nobody else got—and does it matter if you deserved it? How do you feel when others got the discount and you didn't?

Use scarcity mechanics deliberately where they fit, as in Kickstarter tiers, where the fear of missing out on a level that's almost full pushes action—but recognize this is a story you're telling, not a neutral feature.

Decide the policy that matches your positioning before publishing: a fixed-price story supports trust and predictability, while tiered or dynamic pricing trades some of that trust for yield, and the source indicates the trade should be made consciously.
caveats: The Tesla and Uber outcomes are presented as anecdotes about brand perception, not controlled measurements.
The source is explicit that this is largely a storytelling problem for small organizations, not a recommendation for or against dynamic pricing.

Be consistent and patient, and if you can't afford to be consistent and patient, don't pay for brand marketing ads.", "Note how the economics differ by size: Google's and Facebook's revenue growth comes from ads that pay for themselves—$100 of online advertising generating $125 in profit means buying more until ads stop paying—while many large brand advertisers (Ford, Absolut, Palmolive; P&G's Tide and Crest on TV) can't construct direct campaigns that work, and local businesses hooked on Yellow Pages struggle to move to review platforms that feel uncontrolled and unproven."], "caveats": ["The $80 CPM and $100-to-$125 examples are illustrations of the math, not benchmarks for any product category.", "Google, Facebook and Meta ad interfaces and measurement options change frequently; verify current capabilities and attribution in the ad platform before relying on any specific setup.", "The instruction to 'refuse to measure' brand marketing is the source's opinion and conflicts with common practice—hold brand and direct to different standards rather than applying the same scorecard."], "tags": ["brand", "paid-acquisition", "measurement", "media-planning", "conversion-optimization", "creative-strategy"]}, {"title": "Build frequency before judging a message dead", "summary": "People trust what they rehearse, so campaigns that seem stale to you may only just be landing with your market—quitting during the dip forfeits the trust the repetition was building.", "use_when": "Deciding whether to refresh ad creative, retire a tagline, change a packaging story or abandon a channel that hasn't produced results yet.", "steps": ["Accept the memory reality: people don't remember what they read, hear or even see, and aren't good at remembering what they do. That means owning the branded result for your name and product names, not just the category term.", "Translate this into store decisions: distinctive products, ownable product names and a brand people remember are the SEO assets; generic category keywords are a bidding war, not a moat."], "caveats": ["This is the source's argument, framed as a mathematical objection to generic SEO; it does not deny that category search can drive sales for some businesses—the source acknowledges the locksmith, hotel or doctor gains a huge profit from a generic win.", "No keyword volumes, ranking factors or measurement methods are given."], "tags": ["brand", "seo", "search", "product-selection", "acquisition", "differentiation"]}, {"title": "Price as positioning signal, not just revenue math", "summary": "Price tells a story about who you are for, and the margin it creates funds the outbound marketing that gets you noticed—so the number is a positioning decision before it's a spreadsheet cell.", "use_when": "Setting price points, launching a premium or value line, or deciding whether to compete on cheapest price.", "steps": ["Start from the two-way rule: marketing changes your pricing, and pricing changes your marketing. People form assumptions and associations from the price, and the price shapes what they believe about the service.", "Check alignment: your price should match the extremes you claimed in positioning. Note that asking who buys the cheapest or the most expensive wine says nothing about taste or value—only price, which is itself the signal. A Porsche Cayenne has no utility proportionate to its expense; it's a flag flown in the driveway and in self-esteem.", "Run the margin arithmetic before choosing the position. The source's baker: costs of $1.95 per loaf at reasonable quantity yield a nickel profit at $2.00, fifty-five cents at $2.50 (an eleven-fold increase, over 1,000% more profit per loaf), and over a dollar at $3.00—more than twenty times the first example. The $2.00 baker must sell twenty-one loaves for every loaf the luxury baker sells.", "Decide what the higher price is actually buying the customer, using concrete trade-offs: a sparkling clean shop, well-paid and helpful staff, a new window sign, a local baseball team in jerseys with your logo, a handsome shopping bag with every loaf, free butter-cookie samples, and the social pleasure of telling friends they're eating the same bread as the fancy restaurant down the street. The source's framing: better to apologize for the price once than to excuse a hundred small slights again and again.", "Recognize that racing to be cheapest means you're not investing sufficiently in change—you're promising the same, but cheaper. The source notes the race to the bottom is tempting because nothing is easier to sell than cheaper, but that ease is the trap. (This is the source's opinion, offered with the caveat 'unless you've found an extraordinary new way to deliver your product or service.')", "Remember that margin is the money available for outbound marketing—the price position and the marketing budget are one decision, not two."], "caveats": ["The baker's cost and profit figures are an illustrative example, not a benchmark for any category.", "The claim that low price signals insufficient investment in change is the source's opinion with a stated exception for genuinely novel delivery; it is not proof that low-price strategies fail."], "tags": ["brand", "pricing", "positioning", "margin", "product-page", "offer-design"]}, {"title": "Handle price discrimination with story, not mechanics", "summary": "The price tag itself was an innovation built on treating buyers equally, and the source says the hard part of variable or dynamic pricing today is the storytelling, not the implementation.", "use_when": "Planning discounts, member pricing, dynamic pricing, flash sales, Kickstarter-style tiers or loyalty pricing—and anticipating customer reaction.", "steps": ["Take the historical frame: Quakers originated the fixed price tag because charging different people different prices felt immoral; Macy's and Wanamaker's scaled it because they needed huge stores with low-paid staff and couldn't train or trust that many people to haggle. Industrialists liked the efficiency.", "Recognize what the internet changed: on one hand, a store can tell the story that the price is the price—the source cites Tesla, whose fixed pricing luxury buyers reportedly greeted with relief. On the other, matching price to demand cost Uber billions in brand trust, per the source.", "For most organizations, especially small ones, the difficulty isn't the mechanics of charging different amounts—it's the storytelling.", "Anticipate the emotional questions customers ask: how do you feel when you discover you got a discount nobody else got—and does it matter if you deserved it? How do you feel when others got the discount and you didn't?", "Use scarcity mechanics deliberately where they fit, as in Kickstarter tiers, where the fear of missing out on a level that's almost full pushes action—but recognize this is a story you're telling, not a neutral feature.", "Decide the policy that matches your positioning before publishing: a fixed-price story supports trust and predictability, while tiered or dynamic pricing trades some of that trust for yield, and the source indicates the trade should be made consciously."], "caveats": ["The Tesla and Uber outcomes are presented as anecdotes about brand perception, not controlled measurements.", "The source is explicit that this is largely a storytelling problem for small organizations, not a recommendation for or against dynamic pricing."], "tags": ["brand", "pricing", "discount-strategy", "checkout", "customer-psychology", "positioning"]}]}

u want to market to someone who measures dominion or affiliation, you’ll need to be aware of what’s being measured and why. “Who eats first” and “who sits closest to the emperor” are questions that persist to this day. Both are status questions. One involves dominion; the other involves affiliation. Not simply eating first, but being on the same team as the person who eats first. And getting pleasure out of watching others eat last. Not simply sitting near the emperor, but knowing that you’ll be in his good graces (and those of the rest of the royal court) tomorrow as well. Which is the narrative your audience resonates with? Learning from pro wrestling What is pro wrestling, really, but a battle for status? It’s not just among the wrestlers, but also among the fans. Because when your hero moves up, so do you. If you can see the lens that pro wrestling and its fans use to see the world while they’re at a match, you can understand how some people will view your offering as well. The alternative to dominion is affiliation One can gain status without an oil well or a factory. And one can enjoy as much status by letting someone into the flow of traffic as they can from cutting him off.

 This is the status that comes from the community. It is the status of respect in return for contribution, for caring, for seeing and being in sync with others. Especially others with no ability to repay you. Modern society, urban society, the society of the internet, the arts, and innovation are all built primarily on affiliation, not dominion. This type of status is not “I’m better.” It’s “I’m connected. I’m family.” And in an economy based on connection, not manufacturing, being a trusted member of the family is priceless. Fashion is usually about affiliation What are they showing? What is everyone else doing? Is this the season? Within competitive markets, there is a race to be the dominant voice, but among the customers that make up that market, the position of leader works because the customers desire to be affiliated with one another. The leader provides a valuable signal, a notice to expect that everyone else will be in sync. The goal isn’t winning; it’s being part of the group. Sending dominance signals Uber built its brand on dominance. The first few years of their rollout were marked by contentious relationships with local governments, competitors, and drivers. This signaling aligned with the view of some investors, employees, and users and permitted them to double down on their story and how it was told. There are some customers, partners, and employees who will respond best to a narrative of winning and losing. What kind of company do you want to work for? People who align with one worldview often have trouble imagining why someone would choose the alternative. Sending affiliation signals Marketers spend an enormous amount of time and money on the simple task of sending affiliation signals. How busy is the trade show booth? Who else is at the launch party? Who blurbed the book? Are “people” talking about it (which is shorthand for “Are people like us doing something like this?”)? Affiliation isn’t as focused on scarcity as dominion is, because affiliation admires the network effect. More affiliation leads to affiliation for everyone involved. Abundance is welcome. The affiliated marketer seeking leverage works to prime the pump by sending the right signals to the right people, in search of a cascade. For an investment bank, that means running the tombstone ads with the names of all the “right” firms at the bottom. For a business-to-business seller, that means creating referrals. For a local craftsperson, it means hunkering down in a single neighborhood until a reputation is assured. Dominion is a vertical experience, above or below. Affiliation is a horizontal one: Who’s standing next to me? Affiliation or dominance is up to the customer, not you Do you see the world in terms of winners and losers? Up and down? Or is it more about insiders and outsiders, being in sync, being part of a movement? The way you see the world isn’t nearly as important as the worldview of those you seek to serve. As we’ve seen, their worldview is always stronger than the story you choose to tell. The people we seek to serve have a noise in their heads that’s different than your noise. CHAPTER TWELVE A Better Business Plan Where are you going? What’s holding you back? It’s not clear to me why business plans are the way they are, but they’re often misused to obfuscate, bore, and show an ability to comply with expectations. If I want the truth about a business and where it’s going, I’d rather see a more useful document. I’d divide the modern business plan into five sections: Truth Assertions Alternatives People Money The truth section describes the world as it is. Footnote if you want to, but tell me about the market you are entering, the needs that exist, the competitors in your space, technology standards, and how others have succeeded and failed in the past. The more specific, the better. The more ground knowledge, the better. The more visceral the stories, the better. The point of this section is to be sure that you’re clear about how you see the world, and that you and I agree on your assumptions. This section isn’t partisan—it takes no positions; it just states how things are. Truth can take as long as you need to tell it. It can include spreadsheets, market share analysis, and anything else I need to know about how the world works. The assertions section is your chance to describe how you’re going to change things. We will do X, and then Y will happen. We will build Z with this much money in this much time. We will present Q to the market, and the market will respond by taking this action. respond by taking this action. You’re creating tension by telling stories. You’re serving a specific market. You’re expecting something to happen because of your arrival. What? This is the heart of the modern business plan. The only reason to launch a project is to make change, to make things better, and we want to know what you’re going to do and what impact it’s going to have. Of course, this section will be inaccurate. You will make assertions that won’t pan out. You’ll miss budgets and deadlines and sales. So, the alternatives section tells me what you’ll do if that happens. How much flexibility does your product or team have? If your assertions don’t pan out, is it over? The people section rightly highlights the key element: Who is on your team, and who is going to join your team. “Who” doesn’t mean their resumes; it means their attitudes and abilities and track record in shipping. You can go further here. Who are the people you’re serving? Who are the champions? What do they believe about status? What worldview do they have? The last section is all about money. How much you need, how you will spend it, what cash flow looks like, profit and loss, balance sheets, margins, and exit strategies. Your local VC might not like this format, but I’m betting it will help your team think through the hard issues more clearly. Perhaps you’ve seen the shift When you opened this book, you probably said, “I have a product and I need more people to buy it. I have a marketing problem.” By now, I hope that you see the industrialist/selfish nature of this statement. The purpose of our culture isn’t to enable capitalism, even capitalism that pays your bills. The purpose of capitalism is to build our culture. Once you adopt a posture of service, of engaging with the culture to make change, the shift happens. Now, instead of asking, “How can I get more people to listen to me, how can I get the word out, how can I find more followers, how can I convert more leads to sales, how can I find more clients, how can I pay my staff . . . ?” you can ask, “What change do I seek to make?” Once you know what you stand for, the rest gets a lot easier. A glib reverse engineering of your mission statement isn’t helpful Too often, we get hung up on our purpose, our why, our reason for being. And too often, that purpose is simply a backward way of saying, “I’d like to sell more of what I’ve already decided to sell.” In my experience, most marketers actually have the same “purpose.” To be successful. To engage with people in a way that benefits both sides. To be respected, seen, and appreciated. To make enough of a profit to do it again. That’s your why. That’s why you go to work. Okay, got it. But a better business plan takes that universal need and makes it specific— describing who and what it’s for. It outlines the tension you seek to create, the status roles you’re engaging with, and the story you’re bringing that will make change happen. That’s not your purpose. It’s not your mission.
